newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica National Party loses architect of new era.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica National Party loses architect of new era.

text.p: Roelf Meyer, an architect of South Africa's post-apartheid politics of reconciliation, resigned on Saturday from the former ruling National Party (NP) and from parliament after a dispute over the party's political future.
Meyer played a crucial role in negotiating the peaceful handover of power from white rule, but has effectively been sidelined by party right-wingers who see him as too liberal.
He wanted the National Party to disband before seeking to build a broad, moderate alliance to challenge President Nelson Mandela's ruling African National Congress.

"This is a sad day for me. To come to such a decision entails a lot of things. But at the same time while it is sad it is also a day of opportunities and in the end...I guess opportunities are bigger than the sadness," he told a press conference.
National Party leader and former president F.W. de Klerk said, "It is a pity that he has decided to take this route. There is no animosity (between us)".

The National Party was formed as an unashamedly white nationalist group and started implementing apartheid after winning power in 1948. Despite many efforts since the early 1990s, it has had difficulty altering its old image, especially among the blacks it is also trying to woo.
"My argument was that you cannot expect the people to believe you if you don't change," Meyer said.
De Klerk said their fundamental dispute was not over a new movement which could develop into a new party.

"That (a new movement) is the policy of the National Party. But then a perception has arisen and there are adherents to a concept that we could disband at a fairly early stage and disappear into a new party. And that's where the difference lies."

Meyer said he would not join another political party. He told foreign journalists on Friday that the multi-racial democracy propounded in the post-apartheid constitution demanded a breakup of the old order.
He said a new movement would not necessarily be viable by the general elections scheduled for 1999, but it would be feasible to lay its foundations.
Meyer and the African National Congress's Cyril Ramaphosa led the negotiations leading to the first all-race polls in April 1994.
The NP came a distant second to Mandela's ANC in the polls, having failed to broaden its support beyond the white and coloured (mixed-race) communities. It is now the largest opposition party.
